prepared_submissions.message: Batch FAISS uint8 candidate reconstruction before rescoring
prepared_submissions.head: ceba445678cdbda149cac7e8090d329f017e2d34
prepared_submissions.title: Batch FAISS uint8 candidate reconstruction before rescoring
prepared_submissions.body:
## Change

Batch reconstruction of uint8 FAISS candidates before rescoring, using the floating-point index's native `reconstruct_batch` API. The current nested Python loop makes one call per retrieved vector. Binary indexes keep their existing per-vector path because they do not expose this API.

This was found through code analysis and measured with real FAISS indexes. The change preserves candidate selection, calibration, returned keys/scores, and filtering of padded `-1` results. It builds on the scalar rescoring calibration in #4058 and the padding handling in #3887; it does not propose a new quantization scheme.

## Validation

[Independent CPU validation and benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43903476519/job/133425986469) checks unchanged base `9ac7fdb4` and exact candidate `ceba4456`.

- 13 new compatibility cases pass on both revisions: Flat, HNSW and IDMap indexes, noncontiguous document keys, single/multiple queries, short result sets and an empty index.
- `pytest tests/util/test_quantization.py tests/util/test_faiss_batch_reconstruction.py -q`: **171 passed**, including real FAISS and USearch tests.
- `pytest tests/util/test_retrieval.py -k semantic_search -q`: **49 passed**, 153 unrelated cases deselected.
- `pre-commit run --all-files` and `git diff --check`: passed.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/f087887f0be0530c2b94c50a8e3e314846a3a2d8/.validation/st-faiss-benchmark.py) measures complete calls against a reused FlatIP index: 128 queries, 128 dimensions, top 50, 2× rescoring, one CPU thread, three warmups and nine timed runs.

| Corpus vectors | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5,000 | 46.75 ms | 22.93 ms | 2.04× |
| 50,000 | 136.34 ms | 112.73 ms | 1.21× |

Every returned document ID and score has an identical digest before/after. This is a synthetic embedding retrieval benchmark, not encoder throughput; no memory or GPU improvement is claimed. Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.6.0 CPU, NumPy 2.3.5, FAISS 1.16.0. The full model/training suite and older FAISS versions were not run.

prepared_submissions.message: Stabilize LambdaLoss gains for finite relevance scores
prepared_submissions.head: 7bc2a876eb80b7a246fafbe7f9425691d97314cd
prepared_submissions.title: Stabilize LambdaLoss gains across finite relevance ranges
prepared_submissions.body:
## Problem

`LambdaLoss` forms NDCG gains as `2**relevance - 1` in float32. Finite relevance scores can therefore produce either overflowing gains or cancellation to zero. This affects listwise training with continuous teacher scores, including unnormalized dot-product scores or scores scaled close to zero.

Found through code analysis and reproduced with the public loss API. With predicted scores `[0, 1, 2]`:

- relevance `[130, 129, 0]`: loss and gradients are NaN on main; the corrected loss is approximately **3.298718** with finite gradients;
- relevance `[1e-8, 0, 0]`: main returns zero loss and gradients despite the ordering; the corrected loss is approximately **6.396224**.

The reproduction and tests use a trainable lookup scorer, not a claim of a production training incident.

## Change

Factor a common power of two out of the gains and ideal DCG, and evaluate the small difference with `expm1`. The factor cancels in the normalized gain. The epsilon floor is scaled by the same factor, preserving its original meaning. Weighting schemes, pair selection and loss reduction remain unchanged.

This is separate from #4116, which stabilized the log-sigmoid of predicted score differences; the failure here is in relevance gains before weighting.

## Validation

[Independent validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43903476519/job/133425987120) checks exact base `9ac7fdb4` and candidate `7bc2a876`.

- New regressions on unchanged base: **98 failed, 144 passed**.
- The same regressions after the fix: **242 passed**.
- `pytest tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_misc.py tests/cross_encoder/losses/test_lambda_gain_precision.py -q`: **354 passed, 6 skipped**. The skips are the existing CUDA-only float16 CrossEncoder cases; CPU bfloat16 checks run.
- `pre-commit run --all-files` and `git diff --check`: passed.

The independent oracle computes gains with 80-digit Decimal arithmetic and enumerates pair weights. It compares both losses and parameter gradients across all five weighting schemes, top-k choices, both logarithm bases, large/small/ordinary relevance values, ties, zero/negative labels, padding, and a non-default epsilon.

Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.6.0 CPU, Transformers 5.23.0. The full repository suite, GPU execution and minimum dependency matrix were not run.

prepared_submissions.head: a08bf4d023f8b9b2de154a45c8dd36234044fd78
prepared_submissions.title: Support mixed tensor and NumPy dtypes in multi-vector scoring
prepared_submissions.body:
## Problem

A bfloat16 MultiVectorEncoder returns bfloat16 tensors when `convert_to_numpy=False`, but its NumPy export uses float32. Scoring those queries against exported documents currently raises a matrix-multiplication dtype error. The same mismatch affects MaxSim, MeanMaxSim and XTR, including their pairwise APIs.

This was identified by code analysis and reproduced through `WordEmbeddings` + `MultiVectorEncoder.encode_query/encode_document`, with no model download. The regression includes that public workflow, rather than only calling internal scoring helpers.

## Change

Promote query and document embeddings to their common PyTorch dtype immediately before token matrix multiplication. Uniform dtypes retain their existing path and output dtype. Masks, normalization, chunk boundaries and gradient propagation are preserved. Applying the conversion before the MaxSim callback also covers the optional kernel route.

The optional kernel API was introduced in #4344. This change handles mixed query/document dtypes produced by the encoder's own tensor/NumPy export options.

## Validation

[Independent CPU validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43908295487) uses unchanged base `9ac7fdb4` and exact candidate `a08bf4d0`, with PyTorch 2.6.0 and Python 3.12:

- On the unchanged baseline, the 40 new cases produce **36 failures and 4 passes** in both environments.
- On the candidate, the new cases plus similarity and multi-vector loss tests produce **245 passes and 6 existing skips** in each environment.
- The selected XTR/MaxSim/ColBERT model tests produce **30 passes**, 126 unrelated cases deselected, in each environment.
- With Transformers 5.20.0 and kernels 0.17.2, the optional kernel suite produces **106 passes and 56 existing skips**. The second environment uses Transformers 5.23.0 without the optional kernel package.
- All repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass in both environments.

Coverage includes float16/bfloat16/float32/float64 pairs, masks, rectangular and pairwise scores, chunking, all three XTR scorers, independently computed MaxSim scores and gradients, and unchanged uniform-bfloat16 behavior. GPU execution and the full repository suite were not run.

prepared_submissions.head: c8af6717da005b8b2b578a0ef72b65bc000db349
prepared_submissions.title: Reduce SPLADE max-pooling inference work before logarithms
prepared_submissions.body:
## Change

For SPLADE max pooling with gradients disabled, reduce masked token logits over the sequence dimension before applying ReLU and log1p. These monotone transforms produce the same maximum, while only the pooled vocabulary vector needs the logarithms. Both padded/chunked and flattened inputs use this path.

Training keeps the existing transform-before-pool order: finite-precision log1p can turn distinct logits into ties, so reordering that path could change which token receives a gradient. Sum pooling is unchanged.

This was found through code analysis and measured using the public SpladePooling module. SparseEncoder.encode already executes its forward pass under inference mode, so normal encoding uses the optimization.

## Validation

[Independent exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43910447407) compares base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `c8af6717`:

- **101 passed** on both baseline and candidate, independently with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**.
- **264 passed** selected public SparseEncoder tests in each environment, covering query/document encoding, decoding, sparsity and the chunk-size setting; 98 unrelated cases deselected.
- All repository pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass in both environments.

Compatibility cases cover both activation functions; float16, bfloat16, float32 and float64; uneven chunks; left/right padding; entirely masked rows; flattened sequences; caller-input preservation; CPU autocast; and training gradients at rounding-induced ties.

prepared_submissions.head: 02fe393c18a24d617819a97d3e22d3a1a8d91726
prepared_submissions.title: Compute tie-aware ADR target ranks without quadratic comparison tensors
prepared_submissions.body:
## Change

Compute ADRMSELoss's target ranks with a row sort and two searchsorted bounds instead of constructing two batch-by-document-by-document comparison tensors. The bounds preserve the existing average-rank treatment of ties, padded documents, infinities and NaN labels. Target preparation becomes O(B N log N); the differentiable predicted-rank calculation remains quadratic.

This changes the current tie-aware target path. Earlier double-argsort implementations assigned arbitrary ranks to equal labels and are not reused.

## Validation and benchmark

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43925134003) compares base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `02fe393c` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. All **121 new compatibility tests pass on both revisions**. Candidate tests together with the existing CrossEncoder loss tests produce **233 passes and 6 skips** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The tests compare the public loss and score gradients against an independent per-query Python rank calculation and float64 sigmoid objective. They cover ties, negative labels, padding, infinities, NaNs, four label dtypes, three alpha values, and different minibatch sizes.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/71ca95fd68df8c3fe2964e57462829611e764a29/.validation/st-adr-ranks-benchmark.py) runs the public loss forward and backward for four ragged queries using a deterministic score-table CrossEncoder. It includes target preparation and predicted-rank work, with two warmups and five timed repetitions. Transformer inference is outside the measured workload.

| PyTorch 2.14.1 CPU query lengths | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 128, 64, 127, 32 | 0.690 ms | 0.638 ms | 1.08× |
| 512, 256, 511, 128 | 9.836 ms | 9.683 ms | 1.02× |
| 2,048, 1,024, 2,047, 512 | 397.69 ms | 239.89 ms | 1.66× |

The independent PyTorch 2.6.0 runner measured 1.08×, 1.27× and 1.68×, respectively. Losses and gradient SHA-256 digests match exactly in every benchmark case. The benefit grows with the document count; these measurements do not claim a whole-model training speedup.

prepared_submissions.head: d6d7b7b50a34378cad386378ec63a3b5720e2bff
prepared_submissions.title: Invert CSR normalization with its stabilized scale
prepared_submissions.body:
## Change

Use the same stabilized standard deviation for SparseAutoEncoder normalization and reconstruction. LN divides centered inputs by `std + eps`, but currently returns the unstabilized `std`; decode and auxiliary reconstruction then multiply by that smaller value. Even an identity encoder/decoder therefore shrinks nonconstant inputs, substantially when their standard deviation is comparable to epsilon.

Return the actual normalization denominator as the `std` metadata. Existing decode, bias conversion and auxiliary reconstruction paths then use the correct inverse factor. The LN documentation and the auxiliary reconstruction expectation are updated to describe that factor.

This addresses a separate denominator mismatch from #4117, which corrected normalized versus raw reconstruction targets. It preserves that raw-target behavior and makes its inverse transform consistent.

## Validation

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43925134003) compares base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `d6d7b7b5` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. The new tests give **30 failures and 8 passes on the unchanged base** in both environments. The candidate plus the existing SparseAutoEncoder module and CSR loss tests gives **64 passes and 8 CUDA skips** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

The 38 new cases cover identity reconstruction at several input scales and epsilon values in float32/float64; a signed identity dictionary through the public forward path; reconstruction input gradients; finite constant-input behavior; and an independent formula for the auxiliary bias conversion. The very-small-variance cases expose the production reconstruction error without relying on random inputs or relaxed tolerances.

prepared_submissions.head: 8453b7d3bcd77718d8f8d54fbd884ed599676b73
prepared_submissions.title: Support reversed NumPy embedding views in scoring and retrieval
prepared_submissions.body:
## Change

Accept negative-stride NumPy embedding views in the shared tensor conversion path. Reversing rows or columns, flipping an embedding array, or using a rotated view currently makes public scoring and retrieval functions raise because PyTorch cannot directly wrap negative strides. Materialize those views before conversion while preserving the zero-copy path for writable arrays with nonnegative strides.

This intentionally extends supported NumPy layouts. The earlier zero-copy implementation preserved the old rejection, and its corresponding compatibility test is updated to the new behavior. Input values, dtype and caller-owned arrays remain unchanged; reversed views produce an independent tensor buffer.

## Validation

The successful NumPy jobs in [this validation run](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43928364207) compare base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `8453b7d3` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**. The 34 new cases give **33 failures and 1 pass on the unchanged base**. Candidate tests plus the existing tensor, similarity and retrieval suites give **423 passes, 39 skips and 1 deselection** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass.

Coverage includes reversed rows, reversed columns and rotated views; writable and read-only arrays; float16/float32/float64; independent NumPy cosine and dot-product ranking oracles through chunked semantic_search; scalar-reference ragged MaxSim scores; and reversed output from a real offline WordEmbeddings SentenceTransformer. A writable positive-stride control still shares its buffer, and every copied case checks values and lack of aliasing.

prepared_submissions.head: aae6927d9b99bc52c1f9f42f650c42d9ddcc49d0
prepared_submissions.title: Batch sparse Qdrant queries to reduce HTTP round trips
prepared_submissions.body:
## Change

Send sparse Qdrant queries through bounded query_batch_points requests instead of one HTTP request per query. A new `query_batch_size` argument defaults to 64. The coalesced query coordinates are partitioned once into row boundaries, avoiding a full coordinate scan for every query. Results retain their input-query order, including empty sparse rows, and `output_index` keeps returning the original client and collection.

No new dependency is introduced: this uses Qdrant's existing batch Query API from the optional qdrant-client dependency.

## Validation and benchmark

[Exact-base validation](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43929490264) compares base `9ac7fdb4` with candidate `aae6927d` on CPU with PyTorch **2.6.0** and **2.14.1**, qdrant-client **1.20.0**, and a real Qdrant **1.20.0** HTTP service. The new batch-behavior and parameter-contract tests give **20 failures and 9 passes on the unchanged base**. The candidate plus the existing search-engine tests gives **40 passes** in each environment. All pre-commit hooks and `git diff --check` pass. Integration tests use the actual in-memory client with duplicate sparse coordinates, empty rows, single queries, three input dtypes and several batch sizes.

The [reproducible benchmark](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/blob/14504e8f4e96201ef7e85c3ca6e5bd30ee818640/.validation/st-qdrant-batch-benchmark.py) times the full public semantic_search_qdrant call against an existing 1,000-document index with 256 vocabulary entries and top-5 retrieval. Embeddings and index creation are outside the timed region; sparse preparation, requests and result formatting are included. One warmup precedes three timed repetitions.

| PyTorch 2.14.1, real HTTP service | Requests before → after | Before median | After median | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 32 queries | 32 → 1 | 55.73 ms | 6.37 ms | 8.75× |
| 256 queries | 256 → 4 | 444.03 ms | 46.01 ms | 9.65× |

The independent PyTorch 2.6.0 runner measured 7.21× and 11.63×. Returned document IDs match exactly. Both revisions also match an independent float64 sparse-dot-product ranking oracle; maximum relative score error is `1.34e-7`. Server scores between the separately built indexes differ by at most `3e-7` absolute, so the benchmark records these differences and checks a derived float32 multiply-and-accumulate bound instead of requiring bitwise-identical scores.

The [same-runner in-memory control](https://github.com/Afloat16/geoopt/actions/runs/43930174569/job/133520165250) has no HTTP round trips to remove: 32 queries take 151.69 → 155.21 ms, and 256 take 1,225.30 → 1,244.30 ms, a measured 1.5–2.3% slowdown. Its complete result digests match exactly. The principal benefit is remote Qdrant retrieval.
